body:
## Security Finding

**Severity**: medium
**Type**: unsafe-pattern (development-time access defaults shipped in the installed image)

Risk: security posture (a public-facing default; changing it removes remote login from existing installs that use it)

`elements/tromso/system-config.bst` was written to get a first image booting in a VM, and three of its defaults are still what an installed desktop gets.

**1. The SSH server is on, with password and root login allowed.**

- `system-config.bst:111-114` links `sshd.service` into `multi-user.target.wants`, and `elements/oci/tromso.bst:52` runs `systemctl --root=/layer enable sshd.service` on top.
- `system-config.bst:188` writes `PasswordAuthentication yes` and `PermitRootLogin yes`. Its comment says: "PermitRootLogin is enabled for the initial image; users should create a regular account and disable root SSH in production."
- `system-config.bst:171` gives `/etc/pam.d/sshd` `pam_unix.so shadow nullok`.
- The firewall does not cover it: firewalld's default zone is `lax` (`files/firewalld/lax.xml`), which allows `ssh`.

The same image ships the upstream preset that says the opposite, and the static link overrides it:

```
/usr/lib/systemd/system-preset/openssh.preset
# OpenSSH server is not requirements for desktop applications, users
# should enable it manually.
disable sshd.service
```

**2. The screen never locks.** `system-config.bst:345-355` installs `/etc/xdg/kscreenlockerrc` with `Autolock=false`, `LockOnResume=false`, `Timeout=0`. The comment gives the reason as first boot without a known password; the installer now sets one, and the live ISO writes its own copy in `tromso/src/configure-live.sh`.

All of this is in the published image, `ghcr.io/tuna-os/tromso:latest` (`sha256:2b89f634081fa2b9221d35af67ba3ba20f3d2ad37a056a6fb38e6d3064e581aa`): `sshd.service` is linked under both `/usr/lib/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/` and `/etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/`, and `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`, `/etc/pam.d/sshd` and `/etc/xdg/kscreenlockerrc` read as above. Root's password is locked in that image, and sshd's own default refuses empty passwords, so neither `PermitRootLogin yes` nor `nullok` is a way in today.

## Impact

- Every installed Tromso machine answers password logins on port 22 on whatever network it joins: a cafe, a conference, a university. The only thing an attacker needs is a user's desktop password, which was chosen for a login screen and not for an internet-facing service. With #475 unfixed, that password is also root.
- `PermitRootLogin yes` becomes live the moment anyone sets a root password. `README.md` shows doing exactly that for the development VM (`ssh -p 2222 root@localhost`, password `tromso`).
- A laptop that is closed and reopened, or left for an hour, comes back to an unlocked session.

## Recommendation

The owner needs to choose, because options A and B change what existing installs do on their next update.

Option A: Ship sshd off, key-friendly when turned on, and restore the lock. Remove the `multi-user.target.wants` link and the `systemctl enable` line so the upstream preset applies; keep the unit, `sshd_config` and PAM file so `systemctl enable --now sshd` works; set `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password`; drop `nullok`; delete the `kscreenlockerrc` override so Plasma's default lock returns. `just generate-bootable-image` enables sshd in the VM image it prepares, where it already sets the root password and key. Cost: an existing install that is reached over SSH loses that at the next update until someone enables the service locally.
Option B: Keep sshd on, harden it, and restore the lock. Set `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password`, drop `nullok`, delete the `kscreenlockerrc` override. Password logins for ordinary users stay reachable from the network. Cost: none for remote users; the main exposure stays.
Option C: Change nothing in the image and state these defaults under "Security Model" in `SECURITY.md`, with the commands to turn sshd off and the lock on.

Recommended: A, because the image already carries the upstream preset that disables sshd on a desktop, no `:stable` tag has been published yet so the installed base that depends on the current default is as small as it will ever be, and it is the only option that removes the network exposure.

The live ISO is unaffected by any option: its debug build enables sshd through its own preset and link, and the install E2E scripts log in to that, not to the installed system.

Completion, once an option is chosen (A or B):

- [ ] `sshd_config` no longer allows root password login, and `/etc/pam.d/sshd` has no `nullok`
- [ ] the installed image has no `kscreenlockerrc` that turns the lock off
- [ ] (A only) nothing under `elements/` enables `sshd.service`, and the development VM recipe still gets SSH
- [ ] a test in `tests/pytest/` fails if any of these come back
